clue.text: Order accepted for two hamburgers initially — a youth writes it down adding …

definitions.text: Order accepted for two hamburgers initially — a youth writes it down adding …

indicators.note: put in order, so the letters that follow are arranged afresh
says to take only the opening letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A fast-food worker takes an order for two burgers and jots it down, tacking on the usual upsell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' does two duties in the surface but is the anagram signal: A, then F, T, H (the first letters of 'for two hamburgers'), with A YOUTH WRITES IT DOWN, rearranged. The whole clue describes the server saying the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock upselling question asked by burger-bar staff after taking a customer's order.

clue.text: Make clearly understood in approach to head

parts.note: a drive is the approach road to a house
to home is to head for a destination

explanation.surface: A remark about the way up to the headmaster's house.
explanation.definitionFit: To press a point forcefully until it registers is to make it plain.

clue.text: Brute of a horse restrained by youngsters not using force

indicators.note: says the horse is held inside the young people
the letter for force is left out of the word for youngsters

parts.note: yoof is British slang for young people
F is the abbreviation for force in physics
H is slang for heroin, which is called horse

explanation.surface: A savage horse is held back by young riders without any force.
explanation.walkthrough: YOOF is a jokey British spelling of 'youth'; less F it is YOO, around A and H. In Gulliver's Travels the Yahoos are the brutish humans kept by horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's brutish humans gave the word for a coarse, loutish person, a brute.

clue.text: Gave guidance to the female that's stopped being exploited

indicators.note: the female plugs the word for exploited, sitting inside it

parts.note: used means exploited
her is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman offers advice now she is no longer being taken advantage of.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher is to guide or show someone the way, so ushered means guided them.

clue.text: Pianist's partner getting annoyed: 'They should stop people humming'

indicators.note: worked up and agitated, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A pianist's duet partner gets irritated and complains about people humming along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'humming' means smelling bad in British slang, not singing.
explanation.definitionFit: Products applied to armpits prevent sweat and thus prevent body odour.

clue.text: Prime Minister making real money, it's said

indicators.note: signals the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: true means real and dough is slang for money

explanation.surface: A head of government earning genuine cash, so people say.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre and Justin Trudeau both served as Canada's prime minister.

clue.text: You're better not working with them

definitions.text: You're better not working with them

parts.words: You're better not working with them
parts.note: read as advice to avoid colleagues, but means treatments of resting that leave you healthier

explanation.surface: A warning to stay away from some unpleasant colleagues.
explanation.definitionFit: Courses of treatment by enforced idleness that restore a patient's health.

clue.text: Cause upset during week overseas

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters run backwards
says the letters lie inside the run of words week overseas

explanation.surface: Something caused a disturbance during a week abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The run EKOVE spans 'wEEK OVErseas'; 'upset' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke a feeling is to bring it about, to cause it.

clue.text: See 1
Skier's result?

parts.note: a skier sent flying up the slope after a jump could be said to have shot up; the word also means outcome

explanation.surface: Asking how a skier fared in a race.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome or final result is commonly called this, and a skier launched upward literally does it.

clue.text: Diversion taking out the French actress

indicators.note: says the following French article is removed from the actress's surname

parts.note: Frances de la Tour is an English stage and screen actress (Rising Damp, The History Boys)
la is a French word for the

explanation.surface: A distraction involving the removal of some French actress from a production.
explanation.walkthrough: Frances de la Tour is a British actress best known in Britain for the sitcom Rising Damp; drop LA from her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A roundabout route taken to avoid a blocked road is a diversion.

clue.text: He'll be telling you what to do before long, right?

definitions.text: He'll be telling you what to do

parts.note: pre- is a prefix meaning before
to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.surface: A bossy person who will soon be lecturing you, won't they?
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman delivering sermons spends his time instructing people how to live.

clue.text: Think my new team's been accepted

indicators.note: says the new team is taken into the exclamation, which goes around it

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise like my!
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: Someone muses that their freshly formed team has been admitted to a league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is the exclamation, not a possessive; COR is British slang for 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder or weigh something up is to think about it.

clue.text: Picture of Soho criminal and local police

annotationWithheld.why: Picture of Soho criminal and local police (5-2-2) for SHOOTEMUP: an anagram of SOHO gives SHOO, but no parse found for TEMUP from 'and local police'
annotationWithheld.clue: Picture of Soho criminal and local police

clue.text: Trouble about entering most northerly island

indicators.note: says the word for about goes inside the island's name

parts.note: Unst in Shetland is the most northerly inhabited island of the UK
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Disturbance on the remote northern tip of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrest is civil disturbance, a kind of trouble.

clue.text: Frenchman with female is the right size for mounting — Viagra?

indicators.note: in a down clue mounting means rising, so the pieces read upwards

parts.note: Rene is a French man's name
something that fits is the right size

explanation.surface: A risque line about a French couple, sizes and a little blue pill.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, hence the question mark; the whole charade RENE F FITS reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The drug causes stiffening, so it is jokingly a thing that makes rigid.

clue.text: Done by running further

indicators.note: running as in running loose, so the letters of the two words before it are freely rearranged

explanation.surface: Something completed by going further on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Going past a point or more distant means further on.

clue.text: Land seemed neglected around north

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the abbreviation for north
left uncared for and in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some property up north appeared to be uncared for.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic term for an estate's land held by its lord.

clue.text: Rejected swim with old rats rotting in canal by here

indicators.note: says the old rats are placed inside the turned-round swim
turned back, so the word for swim reads backwards

parts.note: a dip is a short swim

indicators.note: decaying, so the letters of rats are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone refuses a dip because dead rats float in the canal nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' turns the swim round, and 'rotting' jumbles the rats; the old rats then sit 'in' it. The definition leans on 'here': the port is by the Suez Canal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian port city sits at the northern entrance of the Suez Canal, so it is a place by the canal.

clue.text: Boris reportedly supporting most of left-wing book

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece below supports the one above, so it comes second
the last letter of the word for left-wing is dropped

parts.note: red means left-wing or socialist

indicators.note: signals the tennis player's name is judged by its sound

parts.note: Boris Becker, the German tennis champion

explanation.surface: A former prime minister backs a largely socialist publication.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris is the tennis player Becker, not a politician; his surname is said like BECCA.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphne du Maurier's best-known novel bears this title.

clue.text: 75 per cent added — watch this fellow

parts.note: more means added or extra; three of its four letters, 75 per cent, are kept
a timer is a clock or watch

explanation.surface: A note about a three-quarter surcharge, then a warning to watch someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's given name or surname, so this fellow is a person called by that name.

clue.text: Comedian saying nothing about American icon

indicators.note: turned about, so the name reads backwards

parts.note: Harpo Marx was the Marx brother who never spoke on screen

explanation.surface: A silent comic turns his back on a US celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: Talk-show host Winfrey is a famous figure of American television.

clue.text: Facilities not very nice — go elsewhere

parts.note: bog is British slang for a toilet, the facilities
food that is off has gone bad, so it is not very nice

explanation.surface: A complaint that the toilets are grim, so take your custom elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A rude British imperative telling someone to clear off, that is, go away.

clue.text: Good seat but he's not happy

parts.note: the rump is the backside, the part you sit on

explanation.surface: A grumble that someone's chair is fine but he still complains.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad-tempered, sulky person is someone who is not happy.

clue.text: Plods at centre investigate scams

indicators.note: takes the middle letter of the word investigate

parts.note: a ramp is British slang for a swindle or racket

explanation.surface: Police officers at the heart of an inquiry into fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plods' looks like the British slang for police officers, but it is a verb here: walks heavily. RAMP is British slang for a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk with heavy steps, which is to plod.

clue.text: Piece of music's rap — switch off radio!

indicators.note: heard off the radio, so the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: a rap is a knock on a door, and to switch something is to turn it

explanation.surface: Someone hears a rap track and wants the radio turned off.
explanation.definitionFit: A short dreamy composition, often for piano, as written by Chopin.

clue.text: Young upstart hit a paparazzo

parts.note: to whip is to hit
per means a, as in so much a head
a snapper is a press photographer

explanation.surface: A cheeky youngster lashes out at a pushy photographer.
explanation.definitionFit: A presumptuous, impertinent young person is an insolent upstart.
